directAnswer: Pope Innocent IV was Sinibaldo Fieschi of Genoa, a leading canon lawyer who reigned from 1243 to 1254. He fled to Lyon, where the First Council of Lyon in 1245 declared Emperor Frederick II deposed, sent friars as envoys to the Mongols, approved the Rule of St. Clare, and issued the bull Ad extirpanda permitting torture in heresy trials.

paras: Sinibaldo belonged to the Fieschi family, counts of Lavagna in the Republic of Genoa. He studied and taught law at Bologna and wrote a commentary on the Decretals of Gregory IX that made him one of the most influential canonists of the Middle Ages; later jurists often credited him with the idea of a corporation as a legal person. Gregory IX made him a cardinal and vice-chancellor of the Roman Church.
After the long vacancy that followed Celestine IV's death, he was elected at Anagni on June 25, 1243.

sections.h2: Flight to Lyon and the Deposition of Frederick II
paras: Negotiations with Frederick II failed, and in 1244 Innocent escaped secretly to Genoa and then to Lyon, beyond the emperor's reach. There he convened the First Council of Lyon, counted as the thirteenth ecumenical council. On July 17, 1245, the council declared Frederick deposed and his subjects freed from their allegiance. The council also addressed the Mongol threat and support for the Latin East. Tradition holds that the red hat was first given to cardinals at this time.

The struggle continued after Frederick's death in 1250 against his sons Conrad IV and Manfred. Innocent returned to Italy in 1251 and spent his last years trying to secure the Kingdom of Sicily for a ruler loyal to the Holy See.

sections.h2: Envoys to the Mongols and New Saints
paras: In 1245 Innocent sent the Franciscan John of Plano Carpini on a long journey to the court of the Mongol Great Khan, carrying letters urging peace and the Christian faith. Other missions, including Dominicans, were sent by different routes. Carpini's account of his journey became one of the earliest European descriptions of the Mongols.

Innocent canonized St. Peter of Verona in 1253, less than a year after his martyrdom, and St. Stanislaus of Kraków the same year. On August 9, 1253, he approved the Rule written by St. Clare of Assisi, the first rule for women religious written by a woman, two days before her death.

In May 1252 Innocent issued the bull Ad extirpanda, which directed civil authorities in Italian cities to set up machinery for prosecuting heresy and allowed them to use torture to obtain confessions, provided it did not cause loss of limb or death. The decree marked a dark turn in the history of the inquisition, and the Church has since acknowledged the wrongs committed in the name of faith during such proceedings.
Innocent IV died at Naples on December 7, 1254.

keyFacts: Personal name: Sinibaldo Fieschi, of Genoa
Leading canon lawyer, author of a commentary on the Decretals
Convened the First Council of Lyon (1245), which declared Frederick II deposed
Approved the Rule of St. Clare (August 9, 1253)
Issued Ad extirpanda (1252) permitting torture in heresy cases

faqs.question: Why did Innocent IV hold a council at Lyon?
faqs.answer: Frederick II's power in Italy made Rome unsafe, so Innocent fled to Lyon in 1244. The council there in 1245 declared the emperor deposed.

faqs.question: What did the bull Ad extirpanda allow?
faqs.answer: Issued in 1252, it permitted civil authorities prosecuting heresy to use torture to obtain confessions, within limits that forbade causing death or loss of limb.

faqs.question: What was Innocent IV's connection to St. Clare?
faqs.answer: He visited Clare in her final illness and approved her Rule on August 9, 1253, two days before she died.
